source.title: On the creation of narrow AI: hierarchy and nonlocality of neural network skills
source.authors: Eric J. Michaud; Asher Parker-Sartori; Max Tegmark

record.tranche_reason: Tests recovery and persistence of skills after pruning, rather than the original gradient-ascent, RMU, or other named unlearning methods.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports benchmark accuracy before and after fine-tuning pruned Llama-3.2-1B models on each benchmark's training set. These are recorded as separate rows. The paper also describes CMSP recovery after pruning in Figure 3; it gives qualitative results rather than numeric values. Other pruning-versus-distillation comparisons do not test a version of the claim.
record.test_reason: The study prunes Llama-3.2-1B toward Python to remove non-Python skills. It then attacks this pruning-based unlearning by fine-tuning on each benchmark's training set (Table 1), and reports accuracy before and after. This is a relearning-attack test (B) of whether an unlearning method's removal holds (A), using a method other than the original sources' recipes.
record.authors_conclusion: Incorrect in emphasis. The authors say all pruning techniques, including random pruning, robustly unlearn non-Python skills with similar effectiveness, except that attribution pruning at low sparsity achieves little unlearning. They note this contrasts with CMSP, where group lasso gave stronger unlearning than naive pruning. They do not discuss counterfact recovery.
record.recipe_differences: Uses neuron pruning (random, attribution-based, or group-lasso) followed by benchmark fine-tuning, rather than the named unlearning recipes. The recovery fine-tuning uses the benchmark's training set; in the CMSP case, it uses the retained task.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies by benchmark, pruning method, and sparsity. On CMSP, the authors say entanglement and recovery vary by seed and width.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy CMSP MLPs, naive ablation-score pruning often leaves the unwanted subtask {3,4,5} recoverable with 1000 steps of training on the retained task; this is seed- and width-dependent. After group-lasso regularization, {3,4,5} is not recoverable at any sparsity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small synthetic networks, pruning-based unlearning leaves entangled skills recoverable, while group-sparsity regularization makes removal robust to retraining.

record.problems: The LLM unlearning experiment uses one model. The text does not report uncertainty estimates for Table 1. The authors say LLM hyperparameters were not optimally scaled and that their attribution pruning is simple. Table 1 fine-tunes on benchmark training sets, but does not state their sizes; the results therefore do not establish recovery from a small set.
record.rows_left_out: No Table 1 entries omitted. Other pruning and language-model comparisons do not measure recovery of forgotten knowledge. CMSP results beyond the qualitative Figure 3 finding are not separately recorded where individual seed/width outcomes are shown only as curves without stated numerical values.

untested.parts: Retention of general/target (Python) ability for the exact Table 1 models is not reported alongside the unlearning results. No named unlearning method (RMU, gradient ascent, WHP) is tested.
The size of the relearning set is not stated, so recovery from a 'small' set is untested. No unrelated or loosely related relearning data is used.
Pruning is presented as a narrowing/unlearning method, and its fine-tuning resistance on WMDP/ARC could bear on F. Only the relearning attack is tried, and no other attacks.

record.verdict_notes: Row states are written relative to B (recovery observed); for A the reading inverts. Chance on these 4-way multiple-choice benchmarks is about 0.25, and fine-tuning values at or below 0.30 are treated as no recovery. The base model itself gains from benchmark fine-tuning (counterfact 0.18→0.49, WMDP Bio 0.52→0.62), so part of any post-FT gain is format learning; counterfact recovery is still read as surviving knowledge. Only one model is tested, with no uncertainty estimates. The best learning rate was selected on the test set. Python retention for the specific Table 1 models is not shown. Record version ids V1/V2 were invalid and are replaced with A/B.

versions.untested_parts: Tests pruning and benchmark fine-tuning as a robustness check, not the named unlearning methods. The table does not establish retention of general ability as a whole; Python performance is studied separately in the pruning experiments.

Fine-tuning is on benchmark training sets or, in the CMSP example, another task. The text does not state that the benchmark training sets are small; it does not test rephrasing, quantization, or recovery with unrelated examples in the LLM experiments.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis demonstrating that an unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context-information recovery test.
No newer method is tested for resistance to the attacks in the claim.

source_check.notes: Table 1 matches all 25 rows; there is no uncertainty, and the best fine-tuning LR is picked on the test set, which favours recovery. Row states are relative to B (recovery) and invert for A. Counterfact recovery is partly task learning, since the base model also rises 0.18→0.49.

statements.problem: For this study, all numbers match Table 1: random 30% Bio 0.22→0.27 and Cyber 0.27→0.27, base FT Bio 0.62, group lasso Bio 0.24→0.31. The exceptions listed (attribution 30%, Counterfact) are right. Minor: the group-lasso figure is at 30% sparsity (63%/80% give 0.29), and the statement does not say so.

Numbers match Table 1: Counterfact random 30% 0.00→0.50; attribution 30% Bio 0.36→0.56, ARC 0.35→0.69. Caveat: the base model also rises 0.18→0.49 on Counterfact with fine-tuning, and pruned models reach 0.42-0.65, so part of the Counterfact gain is learned from the train set, not restored.

Matches Table 1: random 30% Bio 0.22→0.27 and Cyber 0.27→0.27, group lasso 30% Bio 0.24→0.31, attribution 63% Bio 0.23→0.34, base FT 0.59-0.67. Attribution 63% Cyber (0.32) falls under 'most cells'. The body is limited to ARC/WMDP; Counterfact recovers under all pruning methods (covered in B.support[7]).

statements.correction: Llama-3.2-1B, after fine-tuning on the benchmark train set: WMDP stays at 0.26-0.34 under random and group-lasso pruning at 30/63/80% and attribution pruning at 63/80%. Attribution pruning at 30%: WMDP Bio 0.36→0.56, Cyber 0.27→0.55 (base FT 0.62/0.59). The 0.22→0.27 example is WMDP Bio, random pruning at 30%.
statements.problem: Unqualified 'neuron pruning leaves WMDP near chance' drops the exception the authors state: attribution pruning at low sparsity achieves little unlearning. The example does not name the method or the subset.
